samples.summary: Single fixed-name, single-use OAuth state cookie breaks concurrent/retried browser logins
samples.evidence: `GitHubAuthGuard.issueStateCookie` (github-auth.guard.ts:147) always writes the same cookie name `wafflebase_oauth_state` at `path=/auth`, and `takeStateCookie` (auth.controller.ts:221-228) clears it unconditionally on the first callback. Consequences on real paths: (a) two concurrent login attempts in one browser (two tabs, or a CLI login started while a web login is pending) overwrite each other's cookie, so the older tab's callback fails `UnauthorizedException`/`BadRequestException` even though the user did nothing wrong; (b) a callback that is refused, reloaded, or replayed (browser refresh on the callback URL, which previously simply re-ran the flow) can never succeed because the cookie was already destroyed on the first attempt. There is no per-login keying (e.g. state-derived cookie name) to disambiguate.

samples.summary: Download failure envelope reports `HTTP 200` when the response is OK but carries no bytes
samples.evidence: `if (!res.ok || !res.bytes)` funnels two distinct failures into one envelope whose fallback message is `HTTP ${res.status}`. For the `res.ok === true && !res.bytes` case (empty/missing body) the emitted message is `HTTP 200` with code `HTTP_ERROR`, which describes a success status as an HTTP error and tells the caller nothing about the real cause (no bytes returned).

samples.summary: Headless login-URL affordance is unusable within the unchanged 30-second callback timeout
samples.evidence: `announceLoginUrl` (login.ts:199) writes the authorization URL to `~/.wafflebase/login-url.txt` for the non-TTY/headless case, and its doc comment states the goal is to stop leaving "headless users staring at a 30-second timeout with no way to continue". But the callback timeout at login.ts:383 is still `30_000` ms and is started before the browser is opened, so a user who must read the file path from a redirected stream, open the file, open the URL and complete GitHub consent will essentially always hit the timeout. The new path therefore does not deliver the behaviour it documents.

samples.summary: Callback-server timeout can reject an unawaited promise (unhandled rejection) when startup fails
samples.evidence: `callbackPromise` is created at login.ts:306 and the 30 s timer at 383 rejects it unconditionally when not settled. If `startCallbackServer`'s outer promise rejects instead (listen error / EADDRINUSE after 3 attempts at 421-427, or a non-AddressInfo address at 406), nobody ever calls `waitForCallback()`, so no handler is attached to `callbackPromise`; the still-pending timer keeps the process alive and then rejects it, producing an unhandled rejection (fatal on modern Node) after the error envelope was already printed. The timer is also never cleared on that path.

samples.summary: State cookie is not cleared on the no-state callback branch, leaving a stale binding
samples.evidence: `verifyCallbackState` clears the cookie via `takeStateCookie` in both the `w.`-prefixed branch (line 181) and the CLI branch (line 192), but the final `throw new UnauthorizedException(...)` at line 210 (callback arrived with no `state` at all) returns without touching it. A pending `wafflebase_oauth_state` therefore survives that request, so the single-use invariant the sibling branches enforce is not uniform.

samples.summary: Race attaching the `error` handler to the spawned browser process
samples.evidence: `const child = await open(url); child?.on?.('error', () => {});` — `open()` resolves with the already-spawned ChildProcess, so if the spawn failure event is emitted before this microtask attaches the listener, the `error` event has no listener and Node throws it as an uncaught exception, taking the CLI down. The doc comment claims the event is absorbed, but the listener is attached strictly after the spawn, not passed at spawn time.

samples.summary: `mode=cli` with an out-of-range port silently degrades to a browser login instead of failing
samples.evidence: At github-auth.guard.ts:98-130 the nonce/challenge checks only run inside `if (Number.isInteger(portNum) && portNum >= 1024 && portNum <= 65535)`. A CLI start with `port=80` (or a non-numeric port) skips the whole block, falls through to the browser branch at line 132, and the callback then completes the *web* flow — issuing session cookies in the browser and redirecting to `FRONTEND_URL` — while the waiting CLI sees only a 30 s timeout. Given the guard's stated policy that a CLI login missing a binding must be refused rather than started, an invalid port should also be a 400.

finding.summary: Single fixed-name, single-use OAuth state cookie breaks concurrent/retried browser logins
finding.evidence: `GitHubAuthGuard.issueStateCookie` (github-auth.guard.ts:147) always writes the same cookie name `wafflebase_oauth_state` at `path=/auth`, and `takeStateCookie` (auth.controller.ts:221-228) clears it unconditionally on the first callback. Consequences on real paths: (a) two concurrent login attempts in one browser (two tabs, or a CLI login started while a web login is pending) overwrite each other's cookie, so the older tab's callback fails `UnauthorizedException`/`BadRequestException` even though the user did nothing wrong; (b) a callback that is refused, reloaded, or replayed (browser refresh on the callback URL, which previously simply re-ran the flow) can never succeed because the cookie was already destroyed on the first attempt. There is no per-login keying (e.g. state-derived cookie name) to disambiguate.

verdict.reason: The described code exists exactly as claimed: `issueStateCookie` (github-auth.guard.ts:147-164) always writes the single fixed name `wafflebase_oauth_state` at path=/auth for both the web (line 133) and CLI (line 124) branches, and `takeStateCookie` (auth.controller.ts:221-228) clears it unconditionally before the comparison. But it is not a blocking correctness defect. (1) The unconditional single-use clear is the explicitly specified, documented and tested invariant, not an inverted/mistaken condition: auth.controller.ts:215-220, docs/design/rest-api.md:357, and tests auth.controller.spec.ts:298-316 and :411-415 assert exactly this. Consequence (b) of the finding (a refused/reloaded/replayed callback can never succeed) is the intended replay protection; "fixing" it would reopen the replay the design closes. (2) Consequence (a) — a second login in the same browser clobbering the first cookie — is a genuine limitation, but its failure mode is fail-safe and fully recoverable: verifyCallbackState throws a user-actionable 401/400 (auth.controller.ts:182-186, 205-207) BEFORE any user record is touched (findOrCreateUser is only reached at :124 after validation at :120); no crash, no data loss, no corrupt state, no leaked resource, and the CLI settles via its own timeout (packages/cli/src/commands/login.ts:383-392) instead of hanging. The single-login core flow is unaffected. (3) The requested remedy (state-derived per-login cookie names) is a redesign of the double-submit binding scheme — design fit of a security mechanism — not a wrong condition, off-by-one, missing null guard, dropped await, or broken invariant in this lens. I also enumerated the call sites of the protected operation: both takeStateCookie callers are inside verifyCallbackState, whose sole caller is auth.controller.ts:120, and every branch returns a validated state or throws, so there is no unguarded path around it.

finding.summary: `opened = true` after `open()` resolves is not evidence a browser opened, so headless users never see the OAuth URL

verdict.reason: The quoted code does not exist in this repository. There is no `opened` boolean and no `if (!opened)` gate in packages/cli/src/commands/login.ts (grep for `opened = true`/`let opened` matches only scripts/agent/rebuttal.test.mjs). Instead, login.ts:61-62 calls `await openBrowser(oauthUrl)` and then `announceLoginUrl(oauthUrl)` unconditionally, so the URL is always surfaced regardless of whether a browser launched: announceLoginUrl prints it to stderr when TTY (login.ts:200-206), and on the headless/non-TTY path writes it to an owner-only login-url.txt and prints that path (login.ts:209-221), with a further fallback message if the write fails (login.ts:222-228). The second half of the claim is also handled: openBrowser awaits the ChildProcess and attaches `child?.on?.('error', () => {})` (login.ts:179-180), absorbing the asynchronous spawn ENOENT that would otherwise be an uncaught exception. The stale login URL is removed after the flow at login.ts:72. Both described defects are therefore not-present as described.
